note: §4.2 requires every metric shown on the site to resolve to a one-sentence definition AND a statement of what a good value looks like. This is the whole inventory, grouped, with the source of each number and the pages it appears on — the site publishes figures from six different places (nflverse play-by-play, Next Gen Stats tracking, licensed 4for4 columns, the operator's workbook, the betting market and the prediction model) and a reader cannot audit a number without knowing which. Definitions for the nine model inputs are the pipeline's own, copied rather than rewritten, so the page cannot drift from what was computed. Route participation, TPRR and YPRR are 4for4 columns published by the operator's decision (docs/STATE.md); earlier notes here recorded them as cut.

groups.name: Opportunity and usage
groups.blurb: Volume, and whose volume it is. Most fantasy scoring is decided here before efficiency gets a say.

groups.name: Route running and receiving
groups.blurb: What a receiver was asked to do, and what he did with it.

groups.name: Rushing
groups.blurb: Separating the runner from the blocking in front of him.

groups.name: Quarterback
groups.blurb: The passing numbers that describe a good quarterback, and the rushing ones that describe a good fantasy quarterback.

groups.name: Efficiency and expected points
groups.blurb: Per-play quality, measured against what an average team would have done in the same spot.

groups.name: Defense and special teams
groups.blurb: What repeats year to year, and what does not.

groups.name: Kicking
groups.blurb: Volume and distance, and the offense that produces both.

groups.name: Market and game context
groups.blurb: The numbers the betting market publishes, and what they imply.

groups.name: The prediction model
groups.blurb: How the model is scored, and what each score is worth knowing.

data.definition: A player's targets as a percentage of his team's total targets while he was active.
data.good: Above 25% is a clear number one option; above 30% is among the league's most concentrated roles.
data.where: Player pages, wide receiver and tight end charts

data.definition: A player's intended air yards as a percentage of his team's total, measuring how much of the downfield passing game runs through him.
data.good: Above 35% indicates the offense's primary vertical threat.

data.definition: Weighted opportunity rating, combining target share and air yards share into one measure of receiving opportunity.
data.good: Shown here as its two components as well as the composite, because the same WOPR can describe a possession role and a vertical one.

data.definition: Targets plus carries inside the opponent 10 — the touches worth materially more than a carry in open field.
data.good: Among backs with 150 or more carries, the median season is 76 and the top quarter start at 93; only eleven of sixty-eight reach 100. A target is worth roughly twice a carry in PPR and a goal-line carry several times one, so this survives week-to-week noise raw carry counts do not.

data.definition: A back's carries plus targets as a percentage of his team's total carries plus targets.
data.good: Lower than intuition suggests: among backs with 150 or more carries the median is 34% and the top tenth begin at 42%. Anything above 45% is a genuine workhorse in a league that no longer has many.

data.definition: A player's carries as a percentage of his team's total carries while he was active.
data.good: Read next to opportunity share: a high carry share with a low opportunity share is a two-down role.

data.definition: Carries plus receptions — everything a player actually did with the ball in his hands.
data.good: Volume, not value. High-value touches is the version that accounts for where those touches happened.

data.definition: Carries taken from inside the opponent 5-yard line.
data.good: The narrowest measure of goal-line trust. Double figures in a season is a back his coaches want scoring.

data.definition: Targets inside the opponent 20-yard line.
data.good: Twenty or more in a season is a genuine scoring role rather than a compiler.

data.definition: Targets thrown into the end zone itself, regardless of where the play started.
data.good: The most direct evidence of touchdown intent. Unstable year to year, so it explains a past season better than it predicts the next.

data.definition: The percentage of his team's offensive snaps a player was on the field for.
data.good: The floor under everything else — a player cannot be targeted from the sideline. Above 80% is a full-time role.

data.definition: The share of his team's pass plays on which a player ran a route, rather than blocking or sitting.
data.good: Above 80% is a full-time receiving role; the median of the twenty-five tight ends charted is 78%. A licensed 4for4 column, published here by the operator's decision — see the tight end page.
data.where: Tight end and running back charts

data.definition: Targets divided by routes run — how often a player is thrown to when he is actually out in a pattern.
data.good: Above 0.23 is top-quartile among the twenty-five tight ends charted, whose median is 0.21. It separates a player who is ignored from one who is simply not on the field.
data.where: Tight end and running back charts

data.definition: Receiving yards divided by routes run, the efficiency counterpart to targets per route run.
data.good: Above 2.0 is elite for a tight end — the charted median is 1.74 and only a handful clear two. Rewards a player who does more with fewer looks.

data.definition: The average distance beyond the line of scrimmage at which a player is targeted.
data.good: Not good or bad on its own — it describes a role. Under 7 is a possession receiver; over 13 is a field-stretcher whose weeks will be volatile.

data.definition: Receiver air conversion ratio: receiving yards divided by intended air yards.
data.good: Around 1.0 is typical. Above it means a player is adding yards after the catch or converting deep looks at an unusual rate.

data.definition: Receptions divided by targets.
data.good: Read against depth of target — 75% on shallow crossers and 55% on a vertical role can describe equally good players.

data.definition: Yards gained after the ball arrives.
data.good: The part of a receiver's production least dependent on his quarterback.

data.definition: Yards after catch against what a tracking model expected given the defenders' positions at the catch point.
data.good: Positive means he beats the coverage he actually faced. This is the version that is about the player rather than the scheme.

data.definition: The distance in yards from the nearest defender when the ball arrives.
data.good: Around 3 yards is average. Under 2.5 with a high target share means a player is being thrown to while covered, which is a compliment and a risk.

data.definition: How far off the defensive back lines up before the snap.
data.good: A small cushion is respect. Read with separation: beaten cushion and no separation is a player winning early and losing late.

data.definition: The tracking-data version of air yards share — a player's intended air yards as a percentage of his team's.
data.good: Reported alongside the play-by-play figure; the two rarely disagree by much, and when they do the tracking source is the narrower definition.

data.definition: Total expected points added on plays where a player was targeted.
data.good: Counts volume and quality together, so it rewards a player who is both used and effective.

data.definition: Rushing yards gained before contact versus after it, separating the blocking environment from the runner.
data.good: A high YBC with a low YAC points at the offensive line; the reverse points at the back.

data.definition: Rushing yards divided by carries.
data.good: The noisiest number on a running back's page. One long run moves it a full yard, which is why the site leads with opportunity instead.

data.term: Rush yards over expected per carry
data.definition: Yards gained per carry against what a tracking model expected, given the defenders' positions at the handoff.
data.good: Positive is a back beating his blocking. This is the cleanest separation of runner from scheme the public data offers.

data.definition: Distance actually travelled divided by distance gained downfield — how much lateral running a back does to get where he gets.
data.good: Lower is more direct. High efficiency numbers describe a back who bounces runs, which produces both the long touchdown and the two-yard loss.

data.definition: The share of a back's carries run against eight or more defenders in the box.
data.good: A high rate is a defense daring the offense to throw. It suppresses yards per carry and is not the back's fault.

data.definition: How long, in seconds, a back takes to cross the line after the handoff.
data.good: Faster is more decisive. Read with efficiency: slow and inefficient is a back waiting for blocks that are not coming.

data.definition: Pass attempts plus sacks plus scrambles — every play that began as a pass.
data.good: The right denominator for quarterback rate stats, because attempts alone quietly exclude the plays that went wrong.

data.definition: Expected points added per dropback, the single strongest per-play measure of quarterback play.
data.good: Above 0.15 is high-end. It correlates with quarterback fantasy scoring at 0.67 — the strongest football input on the quarterback page, behind only fantasy points per dropback, which is partly scoring measured against itself.

data.definition: Completion percentage over expected: actual completion rate minus the rate expected given throw depth, pressure and receiver separation.
data.good: Isolates accuracy from scheme. Positive is good — but it correlates with fantasy scoring at only 0.23, which is the quarterback page's point.

data.definition: The share of plays that gained positive expected points.
data.good: Around 45% is average. A measure of consistency rather than ceiling.

data.definition: Passing yards divided by attempts.
data.good: The oldest efficiency number on the page and still a reasonable one, correlating with fantasy scoring at 0.50.

data.definition: Designed passes where the quarterback ran instead.
data.good: The count correlates with fantasy scoring at 0.56; the rate at 0.24. Volume of scrambling is production, the tendency to scramble is only a description.

data.definition: Rushes called for the quarterback, as opposed to scrambles.
data.good: The most valuable carries a quarterback gets, because they are repeatable and often come near the goal line.

data.definition: Average seconds from snap to release.
data.good: Neither end is better. It describes an offense, and it correlates with fantasy scoring at 0.14 — the weakest input on the quarterback page.

data.definition: The share of throws made into tight coverage, with a defender within a yard of the receiver.
data.good: A style measure. High aggressiveness with high CPOE is a quarterback getting away with it; high without is one who is not.

data.definition: Average air yards relative to the first-down marker.
data.good: Negative means throwing short of the sticks by habit — fine on early downs, a problem on third.

data.definition: How often a team passes against what its down, distance and score would predict, measured in neutral game situations.
data.good: Positive is a pass-first offense. It moves quarterback volume less than intuition suggests, which the quarterback page shows directly.

data.definition: Fantasy scoring divided by dropbacks — efficiency in the units the game is actually scored in.
data.good: The highest correlation on the quarterback page at 0.77, though it is fantasy scoring divided by volume correlated against fantasy scoring per game, so it describes efficiency rather than discovering it.

data.definition: Expected points added: how many points a team adds on average versus what a league-average team would be expected to score from the same down, distance and field position.
data.good: Above 0.10 per play is a strong offense. The definition here is the prediction pipeline's own, so the site cannot drift from what the model computed.

data.definition: Expected points added on designed runs.
data.good: Noisier and less predictive than passing EPA, which is why the model weights it less.

data.definition: The share of plays producing a first down, used as a proxy for play success rate.
data.good: A blunter, more stable cousin of success rate.

data.definition: How often the passing game produces a gain of 20 yards or more.
data.good: Higher is better, but it is a tail measure and swings hard on small samples.

data.definition: The points a team in a given situation would be expected to score before the play, from which EPA is the difference afterwards.
data.good: The baseline everything per-play on this site is measured against.
data.where: Running back charts, Game Prediction Model

data.definition: How often a defense disrupts the quarterback — sacks, hits and hurries as a share of dropbacks.
data.good: The stable half of defensive scoring. Pressure repeats year to year where turnovers largely do not, so it is what is worth streaming on.

data.definition: A pressure look created by threatening more rushers than actually come, dropping one or more into coverage.
data.good: The only 2025 defensive block in the workbook carrying real values rather than a ranking — noted as such on the defense page.

data.definition: Defense-adjusted value over average: per-play performance against a league baseline, adjusted for opponent and situation.
data.good: Negative is good for a defense, which is the opposite of most numbers on this site — the defense page states the direction wherever it appears.

data.definition: How often an offense's dropbacks end in a sack.
data.good: Lower is better for an offense. Carried by the prediction model as an offensive input rather than a defensive one.

data.definition: Interceptions plus lost fumbles per offensive play.
data.good: Lower is better and barely repeats. The model carries it as a rolling rate, which is why turnovers remain the largest gap between what it knows and what decides games.

data.definition: Takeaways minus giveaways in a single game, from the perspective of the team named.
data.good: The single largest driver of the model being wrong: its picks won the battle by +0.82 per game when right and lost it by 0.97 when wrong.

data.definition: Field goal attempts grouped by range rather than counted together.
data.good: Bands matter more than raw attempts once the long-range rules are accounted for — a 50-yard attempt is worth more and is made less often.

data.definition: Attempts per game, the volume half of kicker scoring.
data.good: Kicker scoring needs an offense good enough to reach field goal range and inefficient enough to stop there.

data.definition: The points a team is expected to score, derived from the game total and the spread.
data.good: Above 26 is a strong scoring environment; below 18 suppresses every skill position in the game.

data.definition: The margin the market expects, quoted from the home team's perspective.
data.good: The sharpest single number published about a game. On this site it is also what defines the market's side in the model's case study.

data.definition: The price on a team to win outright, convertible to an implied win probability.
data.good: The model's benchmark: the market's moneyline has called 66.7% of games correctly against the model's 64.5%.

data.definition: The combined points the market expects both teams to score.
data.good: Totals and spreads move in halves, so implied totals land on quarters and carry two decimals here rather than being rounded to a tenth.

data.definition: The model's estimate that a given team wins, before kickoff.
data.good: Calibrated, so it means what it says: across 4,166 out-of-sample games the average gap between stated confidence and actual hit rate is 1.7 points.

data.definition: The bucket a prediction falls into — coin flip, low, medium or high — with the accuracy that band has actually achieved.
data.good: High confidence has been right 74.5% of the time; the coin-flip band hits 49.8%, which is chance, and the page says so rather than dressing it up.

data.definition: The average gap between a stated probability and the rate that outcome actually occurred.
data.good: Lower is better; 1.7 points is good. It is the measure that decides whether a 70% call can be read as 70%.

data.definition: A scoring rule that punishes confident wrong answers far harder than uncertain ones.
data.good: Lower is better. The model's 0.629 against the moneyline's 0.608 is the clearest statement that it does not beat the market.

data.definition: The mean squared error of the probabilities — the average of how far each forecast sat from what happened.
data.good: Lower is better. Read next to log loss: Brier treats a confident miss more gently, so the two together describe how the errors are distributed.

data.definition: The chance the model gives a randomly chosen winner a higher probability than a randomly chosen loser.
data.good: 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect. The model's 0.69 says it orders games well even where it cannot call them.

data.definition: Training on every prior season and testing on the next, one season at a time, so the model never sees the games it is scored on.
data.good: The only honest way to quote accuracy on a time series. Every figure on the prediction pages comes from these folds, not from data the model was fit on.

data.definition: How much each input contributes to the fitted model, relative to the rest.
data.good: Published in full rather than as a top few — and the page names the heaviest inputs it cannot yet show per team rather than implying the chart is the model.

data.definition: Inputs derived from the betting line, included alongside the team-performance features.
data.good: Including them makes the model better and makes it less independent. The wider feature sets tested scored worse: 202 features reached 61.2% and 455 reached 62.8%, against 63.2% for the shipped set.
